title: Why a communication plan helps the project manager
blurb: Explain the benefits a communication plan brings the project manager, from consistent messages to stakeholder buy-in.
question: On a museum digitisation project, two departments receive conflicting go-live dates, rumours spread that the archive will close, and the board says it gets too many reports it never reads. How would a communication plan have helped the project manager?

teach.body: A communication plan helps the project manager make sure the right information reaches the right people at the right time, in the right way. Everything else flows from that: consistent messages, managed expectations, fewer misunderstandings and rumours, no wasted effort, clear responsibilities, stronger support, and a structure to check that communication is working.

items.label: what each audience needs, no more, no less
every stakeholder who needs it, from the analysis
planned timing and frequency, no surprises
a method that suits the message and audience

head: Benefit
What it means in practice
rows: Everyone hears the same, agreed story
Stakeholders know what they'll hear, and when
Effort goes where it is needed
Each message has a named sender
A baseline to check what's working

teach.h: Scenario: the City Museum digital archive
teach.body: Without a plan, Hannah's team updated people ad hoc. Curators heard 'go-live in March' from one analyst, while finance heard 'June' from another. A rumour spread that the archive would close. The board got three overlapping reports a week and stopped reading them. With a plan, Hannah agrees one monthly board summary, a fortnightly staff bulletin from a single named sender, and a Q&A drop-in. The rumours stop and the board starts engaging again.

teach.h: Without a plan vs with a plan
Two ways to get it wrong

rows.label: Over-communicating: reports nobody reads, overload, key points lost
Under-communicating: stakeholders feel ignored, rumours fill the gap
Planned: each audience gets what it needs, so the PM's time is well spent

teach.text: A plan does NOT guarantee there will be no conflict, does NOT remove the need to engage stakeholders, and does NOT mean everyone gets everything. Watch for absolute words such as 'guarantees', 'eliminates' and 'all'. The plan improves the odds and gives structure; it is not a magic shield.

teach.h: Using the plan to monitor and review
items: Check communications went out as planned, on time, from the named sender.
Gather feedback: are messages understood and useful?
Spot audiences that are disengaged or overloaded.
Adjust method, frequency or content, and update the plan.
Core benefit: the right information to the right people at the right time in the right way.
Consistent messages and clear responsibility for sending each one.
Manages expectations and engagement; reduces misunderstanding, rumour and conflict.
Avoids over- and under-communicating, so the PM's time is used efficiently.
Builds support and buy-in, and gives a structure to monitor and review.

summary: You can now explain how a communication plan benefits the project manager: the right information reaches the right people at the right time in the right way, messages stay consistent, expectations are managed, misunderstanding and rumour fall, effort is not wasted, responsibilities are clear, support grows, and communication can be monitored and reviewed.

A.q: Which of the following is a key benefit of a communication plan to the project manager?
options: It removes the need for a stakeholder analysis
It means every stakeholder gets every report
It guarantees no stakeholder will ever object
The right people get the right information
A.why: The plan ensures the right information reaches the right people at the right time in the right way.

whyNot.0: The plan is built from the stakeholder analysis; it does not replace it.
whyNot.1: Sending everything to everyone causes overload; the plan targets information.
whyNot.2: No plan can guarantee stakeholders will not object.

A.q: How does a communication plan help a project manager reduce rumours?
options: Official updates arrive on a known schedule
Stakeholders are told nothing until closure
Only the sponsor is allowed any information
Informal conversations are banned outright
A.why: When stakeholders know when they will next hear official news, there is less of a gap for rumour to fill.

whyNot.1: Silence breeds rumour; it does the opposite of reducing it.
whyNot.2: Excluding stakeholders increases rumour and resistance.
whyNot.3: Banning conversation is neither realistic nor a benefit of a plan.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of a communication plan to the project manager?
options: Clear responsibility for sending messages
A structure to monitor communication
A guarantee that no conflict will arise
Better management of expectations
A.why: A plan reduces misunderstanding and conflict but cannot guarantee that none will arise.

whyNot.0: Naming who sends each message is a genuine benefit.
whyNot.1: A plan gives a baseline to monitor and review communication.
whyNot.3: Managing stakeholder expectations is a key benefit.

B.q: What does the project manager gain from naming a sender for each communication in the plan?
options: Every message is sent by the sponsor
Everyone knows who is responsible
Fewer stakeholders need to be told
Feedback is no longer required
B.why: Clear responsibility means nothing falls between two people and nothing is sent twice in different versions.

whyNot.0: Senders vary by message; the sponsor does not send everything.
whyNot.2: Naming a sender does not change who needs to be told.
whyNot.3: Feedback is still needed to check understanding.

B.q: How does a communication plan help the project manager avoid over-communicating?
options: It sends every report to all stakeholders
It replaces reports with informal chats
It matches information to each audience
It limits the project to one channel only
B.why: By planning what each audience needs, the project manager avoids sending reports nobody reads, saving time and avoiding overload.

whyNot.0: Sending everything to everyone is over-communicating.
whyNot.1: Informal chats are not a substitute for planned communication.
whyNot.3: Using a single channel ignores audience needs and is not the aim.

B.q: How does a communication plan help the project manager build support for the project?
options: Informed stakeholders are likelier to back it
Stakeholders lose the right to raise concerns
Opposing stakeholders are left out of updates
Support is guaranteed once the plan is signed
B.why: Stakeholders who get timely, relevant information feel engaged and are more likely to support the project.

whyNot.1: Good communication welcomes concerns through feedback.
whyNot.3: Signing a plan guarantees nothing; support is earned through communication.

C.q: Two team members separately email the sponsor with different go-live dates. Which benefit of a communication plan would most likely have prevented this?
options: Wider use of video conferencing
A larger stakeholder distribution list
Consistent messages from a named sender
More frequent reports to the sponsor
C.why: A plan names who sends each message and what it says, so the sponsor receives one consistent version.

whyNot.0: Changing the method would not stop conflicting content.
whyNot.1: A larger list would spread the conflicting dates further.
whyNot.3: More reports from uncoordinated senders could make it worse.

C.q: Which TWO are benefits of a communication plan to the project manager? 1) It helps manage stakeholder expectations. 2) It removes the need for stakeholder analysis. 3) It gives a structure to monitor and review communication. 4) It replaces the risk register.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
C.why: A plan helps manage expectations and gives the project manager a structure to check and adjust communication.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the plan depends on stakeholder analysis.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: the plan needs stakeholder analysis and does not replace the risk register.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the risk register has a different purpose.

C.q: Halfway through a project, feedback shows the board is not reading its weekly reports. How does the communication plan help the project manager respond?
options: It forbids any change to the agreed reports
It gives a baseline to review and adjust
It proves the board is responsible instead
It removes the need to report to the board
C.why: The plan is a structure to monitor and review: the project manager can compare what was planned with feedback and change the frequency, format or method.

whyNot.0: A communication plan is a living document and should be updated.
whyNot.2: The plan is not a tool for shifting blame.
whyNot.3: The board still needs information; the plan helps find a better way to give it.

reteach.title: The house extension group chat
reteach.question: You are having a house extension built. Imagine running it with no plan for who tells whom what, and then with one.

blocks.body: With no plan, the builder tells your partner one start date and you another; the neighbours hear about the scaffolding from the scaffolders; your mum rings daily for news. With a plan, you alone update the neighbours a week before each noisy stage, the builder sends you a Friday update, and the family gets a Sunday summary. Same people, same project, far less stress and far fewer arguments.

blocks.text: The plan didn't stop the noise or the dust. It stopped the confusion about them. That is exactly what a project communication plan does for a project manager.

explain.body: The headline benefit: the plan makes sure the right information reaches the right people at the right time in the right way. Every other benefit is a version of this.

test.q: Complete the statement: a communication plan helps ensure the right information reaches the right people at the right…
options: cost
stage gate
level of risk
time
test.why: The plan aims for the right information to the right people at the right time, in the right way.

whyNot.0: Cost is not part of this phrase; communication is about timing and fit.
whyNot.1: Stage gates are governance decision points, not this phrase.
whyNot.2: Risk level is managed through the risk register.

explain.body: Agreed messages, channels and named senders mean everyone hears the same story, whoever is talking. Nothing falls through the gaps, and nothing is sent twice in different versions.

test.q: Why does a communication plan help keep messages consistent when several team members send updates?
options: Only the sponsor is allowed to send updates
Updates are banned until the project closes
Everyone follows agreed content and channels
Each sender chooses their own key messages
test.why: When everyone works from the same agreed messages, channels and responsibilities, stakeholders hear one story.

whyNot.0: The sponsor does not send all updates; senders are named per message.
whyNot.1: Withholding updates would cause rumours, not consistency.
whyNot.3: Letting each sender choose messages causes inconsistency.

explain.body: Stakeholders who know what they will hear and when are less likely to be surprised or to fill gaps with rumour. Fewer misunderstandings mean less conflict, and informed stakeholders are more likely to stay engaged and supportive.

test.q: How does a communication plan help the project manager manage stakeholder expectations?
options: Stakeholders know what they will hear and when
Stakeholders are only told about good news
Stakeholders agree to accept every decision
Stakeholders receive no updates until handover
test.why: Setting out what each audience will receive, and how often, means there are no surprises about what or when they will be told.

whyNot.1: Hiding bad news destroys trust when it emerges.
whyNot.2: A plan cannot make stakeholders accept every decision.
whyNot.3: Silence until handover leaves expectations unmanaged.

explain.body: Planning stops the project manager wasting time on messages nobody needs (over-communicating) or leaving people uninformed (under-communicating). The plan is also a baseline: compare it with what actually happened and with feedback, then adjust.

explain.caption: Relative volume of communication: the plan aims for the middle bar.

test.q: Which problem does a communication plan help the project manager avoid?
options: Holding any stakeholder meetings
Writing a stakeholder analysis
Producing a project schedule
Sending reports nobody needs
test.why: Planning what each audience needs prevents over-communicating, so effort is not wasted on unread reports.

whyNot.0: Meetings are a legitimate method; the plan helps choose when to use them.
whyNot.1: The stakeholder analysis is the input to the plan, still needed.
whyNot.2: The schedule is a separate plan, unaffected by this benefit.
